name: Bipolar Test
tagline: Explore your highs, lows and shifts in mood over time.
intro: This screener looks at four areas linked to bipolar mood patterns: periods of elevated mood, periods of high energy and activity, depressive periods and how your mood cycles over time. Think about your life as a whole, not just the last few weeks. It takes about five minutes and is not a diagnosis, but it can help you decide whether to discuss your mood with a professional.
seoTitle: Bipolar Test – Free online mood swing screener
seoDescription: Do you experience periods of unusual highs and lows? Take this 5-minute bipolar screener on mood, energy and cycling and get a personal report.

elevated_mood.name: Elevated mood
elevated_mood.short: Periods of unusually high, expansive or irritable mood.
elevated_mood.low: Your answers suggest that you have not had notable periods of unusually high or irritable mood. Your good moods seem to stay in proportion to what is happening in your life. That is a reassuring sign. Everyone has days of feeling great or easily annoyed; what matters is whether such states last for days and change how you behave, which does not seem to be the case for you.
elevated_mood.mid: Your answers suggest that you have had some periods of feeling unusually upbeat, confident or irritable. This may simply reflect a lively temperament or happy times, but it can be useful to keep an eye on it. Notice how long such periods last, whether you sleep less and whether others comment on a change in you. A simple mood diary can make patterns clearer.
elevated_mood.high: Your answers suggest that you have had clear periods of unusually elevated, expansive or irritable mood that may have affected your judgement or relationships. Such episodes are a key feature of bipolar disorder, but only a professional can assess what they mean. Please consider talking to a doctor or psychiatrist, ideally with examples or a mood diary. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself, please contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away. Regular sleep and limiting alcohol can help keep your mood more stable.

energy_activity.name: Energy and activity
energy_activity.short: Periods of unusually high energy, less need for sleep, racing thoughts and risk-taking.
energy_activity.low: Your answers suggest that your energy and activity levels stay fairly steady over time. You do not seem to have had periods of needing far less sleep, racing thoughts or taking unusual risks. A stable rhythm is a strong protective factor for your wellbeing. Keep supporting it with regular sleep and a balanced weekly schedule that includes both effort and rest.
energy_activity.mid: Your answers suggest that you have sometimes had bursts of high energy, less need for sleep or a rush of ideas and plans. Such periods can feel productive and enjoyable, but they can also lead to overcommitment or impulsive choices. Keep regular sleep times even when you feel energetic, and wait a day or two before acting on big decisions or purchases.
energy_activity.high: Your answers suggest that you have had marked periods of unusually high energy, little need for sleep, racing thoughts and impulsive or risky behaviour. Together, these are typical signs of hypomanic or manic episodes. Please consider discussing them with a doctor or psychiatrist, as effective treatment and support exist. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself, please contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away. Protecting your sleep is one of the most important steps you can take right now.

depressive.name: Depressive periods
depressive.short: Periods of low mood, exhaustion and loss of interest lasting days or weeks.
depressive.low: Your answers suggest that you have not experienced long or severe low periods. Down days happen to everyone, but yours seem to pass relatively quickly without stopping you from functioning. That resilience is valuable. Keep looking after the basics that protect your mood, such as social contact, movement, daylight and regular sleep, especially during stressful times. If a low mood ever lasts longer than usual, reach out early.
depressive.mid: Your answers suggest that you have had some periods of low mood, low energy or loss of interest that lasted a while. They may have been linked to difficult life events, or appeared without a clear cause. If they recur, track when they start and what helps. Reaching out to someone you trust and keeping a daily structure can soften their impact.
depressive.high: Your answers suggest that you have had significant depressive periods, with deep sadness, exhaustion or loss of interest lasting weeks. In bipolar disorder, these low periods are often the most frequent and difficult part. Please talk to a doctor or qualified mental health professional, and mention any high-energy periods too, as this affects which treatment helps. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself, please contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away.

cycling.name: Mood cycling
cycling.short: How much your mood and energy shift between distinct highs and lows over time.
cycling.low: Your answers suggest that your mood and energy remain fairly stable over time, without distinct swings between highs and lows. Your moods seem to follow what happens in your life, which is how it works for most people. Keep supporting this balance with healthy routines, and pay attention if you ever notice a pattern changing, for example around the seasons.
cycling.mid: Your answers suggest that your mood and energy shift noticeably at times, perhaps with the seasons, after poor sleep or for less obvious reasons. Many people have some natural variation, but tracking it can be helpful. Use a mood app or diary for a few months to see whether a pattern appears, and share it with your doctor if the shifts cause problems.
cycling.high: Your answers suggest that your mood and energy often cycle between distinct highs and lows that are hard to predict and that affect your life and relationships. This pattern of cycling is a key feature of bipolar spectrum conditions. Please consider seeing a doctor or psychiatrist for a proper assessment. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself, please contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away. A mood diary can help you and a professional understand the pattern.

summary: This screener shows how strongly you recognise four patterns linked to bipolar mood changes over your lifetime. Higher scores mean these patterns have been more pronounced. The results are not a diagnosis: mood swings have many causes, and only a qualified professional can assess bipolar disorder. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself, please contact your local emergency services or a crisis line right away.
